q.q: Why do the decks say to 'learn how the mode works — not just the name'?
o: Mode names are not standardized between manufacturers
Mode names are fixed by an international standard
Mode names determine the alarm limits that apply
Mode names differ by patient age, not by maker
q.e: Names are manufacturer-dependent (e.g. PRVC on Servo = VC+ on PB840 = AutoFlow on Dräger).
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: According to the golden rule, how many variables can a ventilator control at once?
o: None — the patient controls each one
q.e: Control volume and pressure varies; control pressure and volume varies.
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: A breath is triggered by the patient but cycled by the ventilator. How is it classified?
q.e: "If the patient controls both = Spontaneous. If the ventilator controls either one = it's Mandatory."
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: In volume control, a patient develops ARDS. What happens?
o: VT stays the same and pressure increases
VT falls and pressure stays the same
q.e: VC guarantees VT; pressure is the dependent variable and rises as compliance falls.
q.src: VC vs PC: the Difference and When to Use Each

q.q: In pressure control, a patient develops ARDS. What happens?
o: Pressure stays the same and VT decreases
VT stays the same and pressure rises
Pressure falls and VT stays the same
q.e: PC guarantees pressure; VT falls with decreased compliance.
q.src: VC vs PC: the Difference and When to Use Each

q.q: PC is set at 20 cm H₂O with PEEP 10 cm H₂O. What is the PIP?
q.e: PIP = pressure control + PEEP = 20 + 10 = 30 cm H₂O.
q.src: VC vs PC: the Difference and When to Use Each

q.q: What is the key difference between the control mode (CMV) and assist/control?
o: A/C allows patient-triggered breaths; CMV (control) does not
CMV allows spontaneous breaths between mandatory breaths; A/C does not
A/C has no set rate; CMV (control) has a set rate
CMV uses pressure support on triggered breaths; A/C does not
q.e: The slide's one-line difference: A/C allows patient-triggered breaths; control mode does not.
q.src: CMV (and How It Differs from Assist/Control)

q.q: A/C is set at 12 breaths/min and the patient triggers 24. How many full breaths are delivered?
q.e: In A/C every triggered breath gets the full preset support; the set rate is a minimum.
q.src: CMV (and How It Differs from Assist/Control)

q.q: How is a patient-triggered (assisted) breath identified on the pressure waveform?
o: A negative deflection below baseline before inspiration
A positive spike just after exhalation ends
A flat baseline before the pressure rises
A sudden drop of the PEEP level to zero before inspiration
q.e: Assist = negative deflection before inspiration; time-triggered control breaths have none.
q.src: CMV (and How It Differs from Assist/Control)

q.q: What problem does IMV (unsynchronized) cause that SIMV avoids?
q.e: IMV can deliver a mandatory breath before a spontaneous one is exhaled → breath stacking, auto-PEEP.

q.q: In SIMV with PS 8, which breaths receive the pressure support?
o: The spontaneous breaths between mandatory breaths
The mandatory breaths that the patient triggers
All breaths, both mandatory and spontaneous
No breaths, since PS is inactive in SIMV
q.e: PS applies only to spontaneous breaths; mandatory breaths deliver the preset VT.

q.q: Why is SIMV usually combined with pressure support?
o: To prevent muscle fatigue and high WOB on spontaneous breaths
To increase the mandatory rate when the patient tires
To guarantee the set tidal volume on every spontaneous breath
To lower the FiO₂ needed during mandatory breaths
q.e: Without PS, SIMV can cause muscle fatigue and weaning failure; PS helps the spontaneous breaths.

q.q: How is pressure support classified?
q.e: PSV = patient-triggered, pressure-limited, flow-cycled — a phrase on NBRC-style exams repeatedly.

q.q: When does a pressure-supported breath end?
o: When inspiratory flow falls to a preset % of peak flow, often ~25%
When a fixed inspiratory time has passed since the trigger, often 1 second
When the preset tidal volume has been delivered
When airway pressure falls 2 cm H₂O below PEEP
q.e: PS breaths flow-cycle, often at about 25% of peak flow.

q.q: Why can PSV not be used alone in an apneic patient?
o: Every PS breath must be patient-triggered
Every PS breath delivers too large a volume
PS has no adjustable FiO₂ or PEEP setting
PS breaths are time-cycled, not flow-cycled
q.e: PS is active only on spontaneous breaths, so it needs an intact respiratory drive.

q.q: How does MMV ensure adequate ventilation?
o: It increases mandatory breaths when spontaneous V̇E falls below a preset minimum
It guarantees the set VT on every spontaneous breath that is taken
It raises PEEP automatically when the measured SpO₂ falls below a preset minimum
It increases pressure support when the spontaneous rate rises too high
q.e: MMV is a "minimum ventilation safety net": low V̇E → more volume-cycled mandatory breaths.

q.q: On MMV with a target of 8 L/min, the patient breathes 9 L/min alone. What does the ventilator do?
q.e: If the patient breathes enough, MMV stays out of the way.

q.q: What does MMV NOT guarantee?
o: That every breath has an adequate VT
q.e: MMV guarantees minimum total V̇E, not an adequate VT on every breath.

q.q: Which mode automatically adjusts inspiratory pressure to maintain a target VT while minimizing airway pressure?
q.e: Board pearl: PRVC delivers the target VT at the lowest PIP possible.

q.q: On PRVC, the patient's compliance worsens. What does the ventilator do?
o: Raises the inspiratory pressure to deliver the target VT
Lowers the inspiratory pressure to protect the lungs
Keeps the pressure fixed and lets the VT fall
Switches to CPAP until the compliance improves
q.e: Compliance worsens → PRVC raises pressure; compliance improves → it lowers pressure.

q.q: On Automode, the patient makes two consecutive patient-triggered breaths. What happens?
o: It switches from PRVC to Volume Support
It switches from Volume Support to PRVC
It switches to apnea backup ventilation
It switches to CPAP with no support
q.e: Automode: sleeping patient → PRVC; awake patient (two triggered breaths) → Volume Support.

q.q: What is Volume Control Plus (VC+) on the PB 840?
q.e: VC+ = PB's PRVC: preset VT and I-time with variable pressure and flow.

q.q: How does Volume Support differ from pressure support?
o: VS guarantees volume and lets pressure vary; PS fixes the pressure
VS is time-cycled and mandatory; PS is flow-cycled and spontaneous
VS needs a set rate and a set VT; PS needs a set rate alone
VS fixes the pressure and lets volume vary; PS guarantees volume
q.e: Both are patient-triggered, pressure-limited, flow-cycled; VS targets volume.

q.q: On Volume Support, the patient makes more effort. What happens to the support pressure?
q.e: Less effort → higher PS; more effort → lower PS, to hold the target VT.

q.q: What does PAV target?
o: No set flow, volume or pressure; support is proportional to effort
A fixed tidal volume on every patient-triggered breath
A fixed inspiratory pressure above the PEEP level
A fixed minute ventilation with backup mandatory breaths as needed
q.e: "With PAV there is no target flow, volume, or pressure"; pull harder → more assist.

q.q: What happens if the PAV % assist is set too high?
o: Apnea with loss of the backup rate and low pressure
q.e: Too high → runaway; too low → excessive patient WOB.

q.q: Which patient is NOT suitable for PAV?
o: An apneic patient with no respiratory drive
A COPD patient who is being weaned
A patient who is coming off sedation
A patient with a variable respiratory drive
q.e: PAV requires intact drive and a functional neuromuscular system.

q.q: How is APRV defined in the decks?
o: Inverse ratio, pressure-controlled IMV with unrestricted spontaneous breathing
Volume-controlled CMV with high rates, deep sedation and no spontaneous breathing
High-frequency oscillation around a constant mean airway pressure
Pressure support with a backup rate and a volume guarantee
q.e: APRV: inverse ratio, pressure-controlled, intermittent mandatory ventilation with unrestricted spontaneous breathing.

q.q: Which settings are used in APRV?
o: FiO₂, Phigh, Plow, Thigh and Tlow
Amplitude, Hz and mean airway pressure
q.e: APRV has no VT or rate setting; Thigh and Tlow set the release frequency.

q.q: How long does an adult spend at Plow during APRV (Hess)?
q.e: Tlow 0.2–0.8 s; 80–95% of the cycle is at Phigh, producing intrinsic PEEP.

q.q: On HFOV, how is CO₂ removal improved?
o: Increase the amplitude or decrease the frequency (Hz)
Decrease the amplitude or increase the frequency (Hz)
Increase the mean airway pressure or the FiO₂
Decrease the bias flow or the inspiratory time %
q.e: ↓ Hz → larger oscillatory VT → ↑ CO₂ removal — "backwards from conventional ventilation."

q.q: On HFOV, how is oxygenation improved?
o: Increase the mean airway pressure or FiO₂
Decrease the mean airway pressure or bias flow
q.e: Oxygenation: ↑ mean airway pressure or ↑ FiO₂.

q.q: How does HFOV exhalation differ from conventional ventilation?
o: Exhalation is active — the oscillator pulls gas out
Exhalation is passive — elastic recoil pushes gas out
Exhalation is absent — gas leaves by diffusion alone
Exhalation is time-cycled — a valve opens at 1 Hz
q.e: HFOV actively pushes gas in and pulls it out; conventional exhalation is passive.

q.q: Which mode gives a target VT at the lowest PIP with pressure auto-adjusted breath to breath?
q.e: Side-by-side table: PRVC = target VT at lowest PIP, pressure auto-adjusted.
q.src: All the Listed Modes Side by Side

q.q: Which mode is listed as historical and not offered on new adult ventilators?
q.e: IMV causes breath stacking; all current ventilators offer SIMV instead.
q.src: All the Listed Modes Side by Side

q.q: What is patient–ventilator asynchrony?
o: The ventilator's breath delivery is out of phase with the patient's effort
The patient's heart rate is out of phase with the breaths that are being delivered
The ventilator's alarm limits do not match the patient's values
The set FiO₂ does not match the oxygen analyzer reading
q.e: Hess: synchrony = breath delivery in phase with patient effort; asynchrony = out of phase.

q.q: Which is a consequence of patient–ventilator asynchrony?
o: Increased WOB and sedation needs, and longer ventilation
Lower oxygen cost of breathing, less sedation and shorter ventilation
Shorter weaning time and less muscle fatigue
Improved comfort and a lower respiratory rate
q.e: Asynchrony decreases comfort, increases WOB and sedation needs, and prolongs ventilation.

q.q: A COPD patient's observed respiratory rate is higher than the rate the ventilator displays. Which of the following is the likely cause?
o: Auto-PEEP preventing some efforts from triggering
A trigger that is set too sensitive for the patient's effort
A leak in the ventilator circuit
q.e: Patient rate > ventilator rate means efforts are missed, commonly from auto-PEEP raising the trigger threshold.

q.q: During VC, a vigorous patient effort pulls the pressure waveform downward and PIP varies breath to breath. What is the problem?
q.e: The ventilator isn't meeting inspiratory flow demand; fix by raising flow or switching to PC/PS.

q.q: A pressure dip early in inspiration on the waveform suggests what?
o: Inadequate peak flow — 'I need more flow'
Too much tidal volume — 'I need less volume'
Delayed cycling — 'I want to exhale now'
A circuit leak — 'the breath is escaping'
q.e: Early dip = "I need more flow"; late dip = "I want more volume."

q.q: The ventilator ends inspiration while the patient's inspiratory effort continues, and that same effort immediately triggers a second breath, nearly doubling the set VT. What is this?
q.e: Premature cycling: the patient's effort continues after the breath ends and double-triggers.

q.q: What is the recommended order for fixing asynchrony?
o: Adjust settings → reconsider the mode → sedation/analgesia → neuromuscular blockade last
Neuromuscular blockade → sedation/analgesia → adjust settings → change the mode
Reconsider the mode → neuromuscular blockade → adjust settings → sedation
Sedation/analgesia → neuromuscular blockade → reconsider the mode → settings
q.e: Troubleshoot and adjust settings first; "Paralytics don't fix problems — they hide them."
q.src: Mode Asynchrony and the Fix Sequence

q.q: What does Hess call a common cause of failure to breathe in synchrony with the ventilator?
q.e: "Anxiety is a common cause of failure to breathe in synchrony with the ventilator."
q.src: Mode Asynchrony and the Fix Sequence

q.q: Why can SIMV itself cause mode asynchrony?
o: The respiratory center cannot adapt to the varying breath types
The mandatory breaths are never synchronized with the patient's effort
The spontaneous breaths are larger than the mandatory breaths
The pressure support is active on the mandatory breaths alone
q.e: Mode asynchrony occurs when the ventilator delivers different breath types, as in SIMV.
q.src: Mode Asynchrony and the Fix Sequence

q.q: What is normal adult inspiratory flow per the Principles deck?
q.e: Principles deck: normal adult inspiratory flow = 40–60 L/min.

q.q: With constant flow of 60 L/min for 1 second, what tidal volume is delivered?
q.e: 60 L/min = 1 L/s; VT = flow × TI = 1 L.

q.q: What are the three control variables per the Principles deck?
q.e: Control variables: volume, pressure and time; trigger/limit/cycle are phase variables.

q.q: What is the 'independent variable' on a ventilator?
o: Whatever the alarm limit is set to
q.e: "Whatever the ventilator guarantees is called the independent variable"; the other floats.

q.q: In PC, which change increases the delivered VT?
o: More auto-PEEP at the same PIP
Lower compliance at the same PIP
Higher airway resistance at the same PIP
q.e: Box 20-5: VT rises with ↑ driving pressure, longer TI (while flow present) and more effort.

q.q: In VC, which change raises PIP?
q.e: Box 20-4: PIP rises with ↑ flow, constant flow, ↑ PEEP, auto-PEEP, ↑ VT, ↑ Raw, ↓ compliance.

q.q: What starts a time-triggered breath?
q.e: Rate 12 → a breath every 5 s; time-triggered breaths show no negative deflection.

q.q: Base flow is 10 L/min and flow sensitivity is 3 L/min. When does the ventilator trigger?
o: When expiratory-circuit flow drops to 7 L/min
When expiratory-circuit flow rises to 13 L/min
When expiratory-circuit flow drops to 3 L/min
When expiratory-circuit flow drops to zero
q.e: Hess's example: it triggers at 7 L/min, assuming the patient inhaled 3 L/min.

q.q: A trigger set at −5 cm H₂O is too insensitive. What results?
o: The patient may not be able to trigger and fatigues
The ventilator auto-triggers from small leaks or cardiac motion
The ventilator double-triggers on each effort
The ventilator delivers an excessive VT
q.e: Too high (not sensitive enough) → can't trigger; too sensitive (−0.5) → auto-trigger.

q.q: According to the deck's memory line, how is pressure control cycled?
q.e: "Volume Control is volume-cycled. Pressure Control is time-cycled. PSV is flow-cycled."

q.q: When does pressure cycling most often occur?
o: As an alarm condition when the high-pressure limit is reached
On every pressure-supported breath as flow decays
On every volume-controlled breath at end-inspiration
On every oscillation during high-frequency oscillatory ventilation
q.e: Pressure cycling most often occurs as a high-pressure alarm condition (e.g. a cough during VC).

q.q: How is Volume Support classified (trigger/limit/cycle)?
q.e: VS: patient-triggered, pressure-limited, flow-cycled — like PS but volume-targeted.

q.q: What is the number one ventilator adjustment for improving oxygenation?
q.e: Pearl: PEEP is primarily an oxygenation intervention, not a ventilation intervention.
q.src: PEEP: What It Is, What It Does, How Much

q.q: How does PEEP improve oxygenation?
o: It keeps alveoli open at end-expiration, raising FRC and reducing shunt
It increases the respiratory rate, raising the minute ventilation and the PaO₂
It removes CO₂ at end-expiration, raising the alveolar PO₂
It lowers the FRC at end-expiration, reducing dead space
q.e: PEEP prevents end-expiratory collapse → ↑ FRC → ↑ V/Q → better oxygenation.
q.src: PEEP: What It Is, What It Does, How Much

q.q: What is CPAP?
o: PEEP applied to a patient breathing entirely on their own
A mandatory mode with a set rate and pressure
Pressure support with a backup rate
PEEP applied only during the mandatory breaths of a control mode
q.e: CPAP = PEEP with all spontaneous breaths; on BiPAP, EPAP = PEEP.
q.src: PEEP: What It Is, What It Does, How Much

q.q: What PEEP level is associated with an increased incidence of barotrauma?
q.e: "PEEP > 10 (or P̄aw > 30, or PIP > 50) is associated with increased alveolar rupture or barotrauma."
q.src: PEEP Complications and the Dangerous Level

q.q: What is the major downside of PEEP?
o: Decreased venous return, cardiac output and blood pressure
Increased venous return, preload, cardiac output and blood pressure
Hypercapnia from a lower respiratory rate
q.e: ↑ PEEP → ↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return → ↓ CO → ↓ BP.
q.src: PEEP Complications and the Dangerous Level

q.q: How can PEEP raise ICP?
o: Higher intrathoracic pressure impedes venous drainage from the brain
Lower intrathoracic pressure increases arterial flow to the brain
It dilates the cerebral arteries by raising the PaO₂
It increases CSF production by raising the cardiac output
q.e: PEEP raises intrathoracic pressure, impeding cerebral venous drainage.
q.src: PEEP Complications and the Dangerous Level

q.q: What is auto-PEEP?
o: Unintentional PEEP from gas trapped when exhalation is incomplete
Intentional PEEP set by the clinician to improve oxygenation
Unintentional PEEP caused by a leak in the circuit or cuff
Intentional PEEP added by the ventilator after an apnea alarm
q.e: Auto-PEEP (intrinsic, inadvertent, occult PEEP) = trapped gas; total PEEP = set PEEP + auto-PEEP.

q.q: How is auto-PEEP detected on the flow–time waveform?
o: Expiratory flow does not return to zero before the next breath
Inspiratory flow has a square shape instead of a ramp
Expiratory flow returns to zero early, followed by a long pause at baseline
Inspiratory flow starts with a negative deflection
q.e: Expiratory flow failing to reach baseline before the next breath = air trapping.

q.q: How is auto-PEEP measured?
o: An end-expiratory pause; pause pressure minus set PEEP
An end-inspiratory pause; plateau pressure minus set PEEP
No pause; peak pressure minus plateau pressure
An end-expiratory pause; exhaled VT minus set VT
q.e: Occlude just before the next breath; e.g. 12 − 5 = 7 cm H₂O auto-PEEP. The patient must be relaxed.

q.q: What does PIP overcome, compared with plateau pressure?
o: PIP overcomes resistance and compliance; Pplat overcomes compliance only
PIP overcomes compliance only; Pplat overcomes resistance and compliance
PIP overcomes resistance only; Pplat overcomes resistance and compliance
PIP and Pplat both overcome resistance and compliance equally
q.e: Pplat is measured with no flow, so it excludes airway resistance; PIP − Pplat = flow × resistance.

q.q: PIP rises from 25 to 40 cm H₂O while Pplat stays at 20. What is the likely cause?
o: Increased airway resistance, such as secretions or bronchospasm
Decreased lung compliance, such as ARDS or pulmonary edema
A tension pneumothorax or a main-stem intubation
Lobar atelectasis or a large pleural effusion
q.e: "When only PIP moves, think airways."

q.q: PIP and Pplat both rise by 10 cm H₂O. What is the likely cause?
o: Decreased compliance, such as pulmonary edema or pneumothorax
A mucus plug in the endotracheal tube or bronchospasm
The patient biting the tube or a kinked endotracheal tube
Water in the circuit or a blocked inspiratory filter
q.e: "When PIP and Plateau move together, think lungs."

q.q: According to Hess, what is the most important ventilator alarm?
q.e: Hess: the patient-disconnect alarm — a low-pressure and/or low exhaled volume alarm.

q.q: Expired VT is lower than set VT on every breath and PIP is lower than before. What is the problem?
q.e: A leak is low on every breath; with air trapping, expired VT is low for 2–3 breaths, then high.

q.q: The low PEEP alarm sounds. What is the usual cause?
o: A leak in the circuit or ETT cuff
q.e: "Failure of the circuit to hold PEEP is usually due to leakage in the circuit or ETT cuff."

q.q: Which circuit type is used on noninvasive ventilators?
o: Single-limb without an exhalation valve (a leak port)
Double-limb with a wye and an active exhalation valve
Single-limb with a mushroom exhalation valve at the patient
Double-limb with a leak port in the expiratory limb
q.e: NIV uses a known leak port; the ventilator calculates and subtracts the leak.

q.q: Where is the exhalation valve in a double-limb (wye) ICU circuit?
q.e: Double-limb circuits carry exhaled gas back to the ventilator's expiratory/PEEP valve.

q.q: Circuit compliance is 3 mL/cm H₂O, PIP 60 and PEEP 10. How much volume is compressed in the circuit?
q.e: 3 mL/cm H₂O × (60 − 10) = 150 mL; corrected VT = expired VT − 150 mL.

q.q: What are the two jobs of the exhalation valve?
o: Separate inspiration from expiration and set PEEP
Humidify the inspired gas and filter out bacteria
Measure the FiO₂ and trigger breaths
Warm the gas and measure the VT
q.e: Closed in inspiration, open for exhalation; the expiratory valve controls PEEP.

q.q: Which circuit obstruction is the more serious?
o: Expiratory — it can cause rebreathing, asphyxia or barotrauma
Inspiratory — it can prevent delivery of the prescribed tidal volume
Humidifier — it can cause overheating of the inspired gas
Inspiratory filter — it can restrict delivery of the set breath
q.e: Expiratory obstruction is more serious; it comes with low-volume and high-pressure alarms.

q.q: Why must the expiratory valve be checked during aerosolized ribavirin?
o: Ribavirin can crystallize and occlude valves and sensors
Ribavirin can raise the delivered FiO₂ and the PEEP
Ribavirin can dissolve the plastic of the circuit
Ribavirin can cause auto-triggering and stacking
q.e: Ribavirin crystals impair expiratory valves and sensors; watch for ↑ peak pressures.

q.q: What does the equation of motion describe?
o: The pressure needed to overcome airway resistance and lung/chest-wall elastance
The relationship between the inspired oxygen fraction and the arterial PO₂
The volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute during a breath
The amount of oxygen carried by hemoglobin and dissolved in plasma
q.e: Pressure must overcome R × flow (resistive load) and E × volume (elastic load).

q.q: In the equation of motion, what is elastance?
q.e: E = respiratory system elastance (lungs + chest wall), the inverse of compliance.

q.q: During full ventilatory support, what is Pmus in the equation of motion?
o: Zero — all pressure comes from the ventilator
Equal to the airway pressure the ventilator displays
q.e: Full support: Pmus = 0. Spontaneous breathing: Paw = 0. Partial: both contribute.

q.q: Which four ventilator modes does the Ch 11 deck say to 'KNOW THESE' for the NBRC?
q.e: Control variable (volume or pressure) × A/C or SIMV; PS and PEEP are add-ons.
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: According to the Ch 11 deck, what are the three categories of patient–ventilator asynchrony?
q.e: Use the deck's trigger, flow, cycle (Hess says trigger, cycle, mode).

q.q: How is adult HFOV weaned per the Ch 11 deck?
o: FiO₂ to 0.40 first; then mean airway pressure down 2–3 every 4–6 h to ≤ 20; then switch to PC
Amplitude to maximum first; then frequency down 1 Hz every hour to 3 Hz; then extubate
Mean airway pressure to ≤ 10 first; then FiO₂ down 0.10 every 4–6 h to 0.21; then CPAP
Frequency up to 15 Hz first; then amplitude down 5 every 2 h to zero; then switch to VC
q.e: Then consider PC (limit ≤ 30, PEEP 10–12) and a standard SBT.

q.q: Where does the Ch 11 deck set the high-pressure alarm before PIP is measured?
o: 35 cm H₂O, then 10 above the observed PIP once stable
60 cm H₂O, then 25 above the observed PIP once stable
20 cm H₂O, then equal to the observed PIP once stable
50 cm H₂O, then 5 below the observed PIP once stable
q.e: Ch 11 (AARC): 35 initially, then 10 above observed PIP.

q.q: Where does the Ch 11 deck set the low inspiratory pressure alarm?
o: 10 cm H₂O below the observed PIP (or the set pressure in PC)
Equal to the set PEEP level (or 2 cm H₂O above it in PC)
10 cm H₂O above the observed PIP (or the set pressure in PC)
25 cm H₂O below the observed PIP (or half the set pressure in PC)
q.e: With the low VT alarm (150 mL above and below set VT), it detects leaks or disconnection.

q.q: The volume–time curve does not return to baseline. What does the Ch 11 deck say this means?
o: A leak — often the ETT cuff
q.e: Likely on the NBRC: find the leak (cuff, connections, humidifier, mask, chest tube/BPF).

q.q: How is static compliance calculated, and what pressure is ignored?
q.e: Ch 11: in a static-compliance table, disregard PIP — "it is there to confuse you."

q.q: VT 600 mL, Pplat 27, PEEP 10, PIP 40. What is the static compliance?
q.e: 600 ÷ (27 − 10) = 35.3; PIP is a distractor.

q.q: What normal static compliance does RCP 203 give for intubated adults?
q.e: Use RCP 203's 40–80; < 25–30 → ↑ WOB and weaning difficulty.

q.q: How does dynamic compliance compare with static compliance?
o: It is always less, the difference being airway resistance
It is always greater, the difference being the applied PEEP
It is equal, because both use the plateau pressure
It is always less, the difference being the auto-PEEP
q.e: Cdyn = VT ÷ (PIP − PEEP); PIP includes resistive pressure.

q.q: How is alveolar ventilation calculated?
q.e: V̇A accounts for dead space; V̇E = VT × f does not.

q.q: A 125-lb patient breathes 15/min with VT 400 mL. What is the alveolar ventilation?
How does lowering VT affect VD/VT?
o: It raises VD/VT and lowers alveolar ventilation
It lowers VD/VT and raises alveolar ventilation
It raises VD/VT and raises alveolar ventilation
It leaves VD/VT and alveolar ventilation unchanged

q.q: How much water vapor does fully saturated gas hold at 37 °C?
Condensate is visible in the inspiratory tubing near the patient. What does this indicate?
o: The gas is fully saturated (100% RH)
The gas is too dry (below 50% RH)
q.e: No visible condensate = RH could be anywhere 0–99%.

q.q: How should circuit condensate be handled?
o: Drained with gloves away from the patient and discarded as contaminated waste
Poured back into the humidifier chamber so that the sterile water is not wasted
Drained toward the patient's airway and removed by suctioning
Left in the tubing until the next scheduled circuit change
q.e: Never let it reach the airway; never return it to the reservoir.

q.q: What humidity does an HME provide per the deck?
q.e: Heated humidifier: near 100% RH at body temperature; HME 70–90% at 30–31 °C.

q.q: What happens if cuff pressure is too high?
o: Tracheal mucosal ischemia, ulceration and necrosis
Hypoventilation from a leak during inspiration
q.e: Too high (> 25–30) obstructs mucosal blood flow; too low (< 20) allows aspiration.

q.q: An ETT cuff needs more than 30 cm H₂O to seal the airway. Which of the following does this suggest?
o: The tube may be too small — evaluate and recommend exchange
The tube is working normally — continue to monitor the pressure
The patient needs more PEEP — increase it and remeasure the cuff
The tube may be too large — deflate the cuff and recheck in 4 hours
q.e: Rising pressures over time suggest tracheal dilation or cuff/pilot balloon malfunction.

q.q: Is the minimal leak technique recommended for cuff management?
o: No — it is no longer recommended
Yes — it is the standard for all patients
Yes — but for laryngeal mask airways only
Yes — but for children under 8 only
q.e: RCP 203 and the VAP strategies: avoid the minimal leak technique.

q.q: What pressure is the King LT cuff inflated to?
q.e: ETT 20–30; LMA ≤ 60; King LT ~60 cm H₂O.

q.q: Rate 15, VT 600 mL, and the physician orders I:E 1:4. What inspiratory flow is needed?
q.e: V̇E 9 L/min ÷ %I-time 0.20 = 45 L/min.

q.q: What %I-time corresponds to an I:E ratio of 1:2?
A ventilated COPD patient has auto-PEEP with an I:E ratio of 1:2. Which of the following should be done?
o: Decrease the ratio toward 1:4 or 1:5 by lengthening E-time
Increase the ratio to 1:1 by lengthening the I-time and adding a pause
Change to inverse ratio ventilation at 2:1
Increase the rate and shorten the E-time
q.e: Severe obstruction needs long E-times; lowering the rate lengthens E-time.

q.q: What is the permissive hypercapnia floor in the Ch 13 deck?
o: pH below 7.25–7.30 — then raise the rate or give bicarbonate
PaCO₂ above 50 mm Hg — then lower the rate or the tidal volume
pH below 7.40 — then raise the tidal volume to 10 mL/kg
PaCO₂ above 100 mm Hg — then switch to HFOV or ECMO
q.e: pH is the stop sign, not PaCO₂.

q.q: What must be programmed into the ventilator to use automatic tube compensation (ATC)?
o: The patient's airway type and size
The PEEP and pressure support levels
q.e: ATC dynamically offsets tube resistance for spontaneous breaths.

q.q: In the ARDSNet protocol, what VT is used at the start and the target?
o: Start 8 mL/kg PBW; reduce by 1 mL/kg to 6 mL/kg
Start 12 mL/kg PBW; reduce by 2 mL/kg to 8 mL/kg
Start 4 mL/kg PBW; raise by 1 mL/kg to 10 mL/kg
Start 6 mL/kg PBW; raise by 1 mL/kg to 8 mL/kg
q.e: Reduce 1 mL/kg at intervals ≤ 2 h until VT = 6 mL/kg PBW.
q.src: The ARDSNet Protocol Step by Step (Ch 14)

q.q: In ARDSNet, what is done if Pplat exceeds 30 cm H₂O?
o: Decrease VT in 1 mL/kg steps to a minimum of 4 mL/kg
Increase VT in 1 mL/kg steps to a maximum of 8 mL/kg
Increase the PEEP in 2 cm H₂O steps to 20 cm H₂O
Decrease the rate in steps of 2 to a minimum of 6/min
q.e: Pplat ≤ 30; measure every 4 h and after each PEEP or VT change.
q.src: The ARDSNet Protocol Step by Step (Ch 14)

q.q: In ARDSNet, the pH is 7.10 with the rate already at 35. What is done?
o: Increase VT in 1 mL/kg steps until pH > 7.15; consider NaHCO₃
Decrease VT in 1 mL/kg steps until pH > 7.30; lower the rate
Lower the PEEP in 2 cm H₂O steps until pH > 7.15
Increase the rate to 45 and stop the bicarbonate
q.e: For pH < 7.15, raise rate to 35 first; then VT (Pplat may be exceeded).
q.src: The ARDSNet Protocol Step by Step (Ch 14)

q.q: What pH goal does the ARDSNet protocol use?
q.e: pH goal 7.30–7.45; PaO₂ 55–80 or SpO₂ 88–95%.
q.src: The ARDSNet Protocol Step by Step (Ch 14)

q.q: What does a recruitment maneuver do?
o: Briefly raises transpulmonary pressure to reopen collapsed alveoli
Briefly lowers the PEEP to zero to let trapped gas escape
Removes retained secretions with a deep breath followed by suction
Raises the rate for 2 minutes to wash out carbon dioxide
q.e: Recruitment opens; adequate PEEP afterward keeps alveoli open.

q.q: Are recruitment maneuvers routinely recommended in ARDS per the revised Ch 11 deck?
o: No — lung-protective ventilation, PEEP and proning come first
Yes — every shift, and before any change in the PEEP level is made
Yes — before every spontaneous breathing trial
No — they are used with HFOV and APRV alone
q.e: Better oxygenation does not guarantee a better outcome.

q.q: How is decremental PEEP titration done after a recruitment maneuver?
o: Lower PEEP in small steps, then set it slightly above where compliance starts to fall
Raise PEEP in small steps, then set it where the blood pressure begins to fall
Lower PEEP to zero at once, then raise it until the SpO₂ reaches 100%
Lower PEEP in small steps, then set it slightly below where compliance starts to fall
q.e: In the deck's example, PEEP was chosen at 18 cm H₂O.

q.q: When should a recruitment maneuver be stopped?
o: If MAP falls below 60–65 mm Hg or the patient deteriorates
If the SpO₂ improves by 5% or the measured compliance rises
After exactly 10 seconds in every patient
When the PIP reaches 25 cm H₂O
q.e: Do RMs only in hemodynamically stable patients (MAP ≥ 65).

q.q: Is there a sourced 'normal' range for adult PIP?
o: No — sources give only ceilings, such as 'safe' < 50 cm H₂O
Yes — 5–10 cm H₂O in every source
Yes — sources agree on 40–60 cm H₂O for ventilated adults
Yes — 25–30 cm H₂O in every source
q.e: Only ceilings exist; Pplat is the one to watch (< 30).
q.src: Normal (Target) Levels of PIP, Pplat and PEEP

q.q: What Pplat ceiling should be used for this exam?
q.e: Conflict: Chang prints < 35; use < 30 (ARDSNet, Hess, Ch 11).
q.src: Normal (Target) Levels of PIP, Pplat and PEEP

q.q: What low-level PEEP is often used to prevent atelectasis in ventilated patients (Hess)?
q.e: Initial PEEP 5 (NBRC range 2–6); 'safe' < 10.
q.src: Normal (Target) Levels of PIP, Pplat and PEEP

q.q: What normal airway resistance does RCP 203 give for intubated adults?
q.e: RCP 203 intubated normals: Crs 40–80 mL/cm H₂O, Raw 5–12 cm H₂O/L/s.
q.src: Normal (Target) Levels of PIP, Pplat and PEEP

q.q: What does PIP − Pplat represent?
q.e: Depends on flow setting and airway resistance.

q.q: Which pressure is used for the < 15 cm H₂O lung-protective driving-pressure limit?
q.e: In PC, VT is changed via ΔP = PIP − PEEP (Ch 11), but the < 15 limit is Pplat − PEEP.

q.q: Why does Pplat reflect only compliance?
o: It is measured during an end-inspiratory hold with no flow
It is measured at peak flow, at the end of inspiration
It is measured at end-expiration with the valves closed
It is measured during a hold that includes resistance
q.e: No flow means no resistive pressure.

q.q: PIP rises while Pplat stays normal. What is the lung condition?
q.e: Bronchospasm, secretions, edema, water in circuit, kinked ETT.
q.src: Lung Condition When PIP and Pplat Rise or Fall

q.q: PIP and Pplat rise together. Which is a likely cause?
o: Secretions or a kink in the ETT
q.e: ↓ compliance (stiff lungs): ARDS, edema, pneumonia, effusion, pneumothorax, mainstem intubation.
q.src: Lung Condition When PIP and Pplat Rise or Fall

q.q: PIP is lower than the previous breath on every breath, but pressure returns to baseline. What is it?
q.e: A leak lowers PIP every breath.
q.src: Lung Condition When PIP and Pplat Rise or Fall

q.q: In pressure control, how does a stiffer lung show up?
q.e: Pressure is fixed in PC, so worse mechanics reduce VT.
q.src: Lung Condition When PIP and Pplat Rise or Fall

q.q: What happens with too little PEEP?
o: Alveoli collapse, causing shunt and poor oxygenation
Alveoli overdistend, causing dead space and barotrauma
Venous return falls, causing a drop in cardiac output
Airway resistance rises, causing a high peak pressure
q.e: Too little → collapse; too much → overdistension, barotrauma, ↓ CO.
q.src: PEEP Too Low vs Too High

q.q: What does the Ch 11 deck call optimal PEEP?
o: The PEEP that keeps SpO₂ ≥ 88–90% without lowering BP
The highest PEEP the patient tolerates without barotrauma
The PEEP of 5 cm H₂O that is used for every patient
The PEEP that keeps PaO₂ above 200 on an FiO₂ of 1.0
q.e: Optimal PEEP balances oxygenation against hemodynamics.
q.src: PEEP Too Low vs Too High

q.q: Is PEEP > 10 cm H₂O an absolute ceiling?
o: No — it is Chang's barotrauma risk threshold; ARDS may need more
Yes — the decks say never to exceed 10 cm H₂O in any adult patient
Yes — but the ceiling applies to patients with ARDS alone
No — it is the minimum PEEP for all ventilated patients
q.e: Ch 11's optimal-PEEP examples are 15 and 18.
q.src: PEEP Too Low vs Too High

q.q: How does raised intrathoracic pressure lower urine output?
o: Reduced cardiac output lowers renal blood flow, and ADH rises
Increased cardiac output raises renal blood flow, and ADH falls
Compression of the ureters blocks the flow of urine
Stretch of the atria raises ANP and lowers ADH
q.e: PPV → ↓ CO → ↓ renal flow; ↑ ADH and ↓ ANP retain fluid.
q.src: Effects on the Body When Pressures Rise

q.q: Why can CVP rise with PEEP even though preload is falling?
o: Intrathoracic pressure raises the measured CVP while venous return falls
PEEP adds to the circulating blood volume as venous return rises
The measured CVP always equals preload, so both of them must rise
The catheter tip migrates into the right ventricle with each breath
q.e: "High CVP does not always mean lots of preload."
q.src: Effects on the Body When Pressures Rise

q.q: Which organ is hit first by falling cardiac output from PPV?
q.e: The kidneys are more sensitive than the liver; hepatic perfusion falls only when PEEP is added.
q.src: Effects on the Body When Pressures Rise

q.q: How can PPV benefit a patient with left heart failure?
q.e: Hess: the drop in LV afterload can help fluid overload or LV failure.
q.src: Effects on the Body When Pressures Rise

q.q: How does the deck define auto-PEEP in the pressures topic?
o: Residual alveolar pressure at end-exhalation from air trapping
The PEEP level set by the clinician on the ventilator
Pressure lost through a leak at end-exhalation
Alveolar pressure at the end of an inspiratory hold, from the set VT
q.e: Aka occult/intrinsic PEEP, dynamic hyperinflation; common in COPD and asthma.
q.src: Auto-PEEP: What It Is and How to Find It

q.q: End-expiratory pause pressure is 12 with set PEEP 5. What is the auto-PEEP?
q.e: Auto-PEEP = pause pressure − set PEEP.
q.src: Auto-PEEP: What It Is and How to Find It

q.q: Which graphic does the Ch 11 deck say is likely on the NBRC for auto-PEEP?
o: Expiratory flow not returning to zero before the next breath
The volume curve not returning to baseline before the next breath
A pressure spike at end-inspiration during pressure support
A negative pressure deflection just before each inspiration
q.e: Volume not returning to baseline = a leak; flow not returning to zero = air trapping.
q.src: Auto-PEEP: What It Is and How to Find It

q.q: Which change does NOT help resolve auto-PEEP?
q.e: Fixes lengthen expiratory time: ↓ RR, ↑ flow, ↓ VT, ↓ TI, bronchodilators.

q.q: How much extrinsic PEEP may be applied to counter auto-PEEP per RCP 203?
o: Up to 80–90% of measured auto-PEEP, in spontaneously breathing patients
Up to 150% of measured auto-PEEP, in paralyzed patients on volume control
Up to the peak inspiratory pressure, in all patients
None — applied PEEP always worsens air trapping
q.e: Use RCP 203's 80–90% (Hess: 75–85%); it helps patients trigger.

q.q: Which axes does a pressure–volume loop use?
o: Pressure on the x-axis, volume on the y-axis
Volume on the x-axis, flow on the y-axis
Time on the x-axis, pressure on the y-axis
Flow on the x-axis, pressure on the y-axis
q.e: The P-V loop is the "compliance" loop.
q.src: The Pressure-Volume (P-V) Loop: How to Read It

q.q: What does the slope of the static P-V curve represent?
q.e: Ch 11: "the higher the slope, the higher the compliance."
q.src: The Pressure-Volume (P-V) Loop: How to Read It

q.q: How does a spontaneous breath look on a P-V loop?
o: Oval and symmetric with no sharp corners
A small trigger dip then machine assistance
q.e: Controlled = sharp angles; assisted = small trigger effort, then assistance.
q.src: The Pressure-Volume (P-V) Loop: How to Read It

q.q: Compliance decreases. How does the P-V loop shift?
o: Toward the pressure axis (right) and flatter
Toward the volume axis (left) and steeper
Upward along the volume axis with no tilt
Toward the pressure axis (right) and wider
q.e: ↓ compliance: ↑ PIP and ↑ PAlv; ARDS, edema, atelectasis, fibrosis.
q.src: Compliance Changes on the P-V Loop

q.q: Which condition shifts the P-V loop toward the volume axis (steeper)?
q.e: Emphysema has high compliance with poor recoil.
q.src: Compliance Changes on the P-V Loop

q.q: What does PEEP or surfactant do to the P-V curve when compliance improves?
q.e: Improved compliance → steeper curve.
q.src: Compliance Changes on the P-V Loop

q.q: What does a 'beak' (duckbill) at the top of the P-V loop indicate?
o: A leak from the circuit or the cuff
Auto-PEEP from a short expiratory time
q.e: Beyond the UIP, small volume rises cause large pressure rises; reduce VT.

q.q: What is the lower inflection point?
o: The pressure where alveoli begin to open (critical opening pressure)
The pressure where the lung starts to overdistend (the 'beak' of the loop)
The pressure in the airway at the end of exhalation
The peak pressure that is reached at end-inspiration
q.e: Below it the curve is flat (under-recruitment).

q.q: Where does Ch 11 set PEEP relative to the lower inflection point?
q.e: Optimal PEEP = the lowest pressure that exceeds the LIP.

q.q: How is overdistension on the P-V loop fixed?
o: Reduce VT until the beak disappears
Increase VT until the loop widens
Increase PEEP until the beak flattens
Increase the rate and the flow
q.e: Or use pressure control.

q.q: On the P-V loop, what does a wider loop indicate (exam answer)?
q.e: Use "wider = more resistance" (slide 74 notes; RCP 203 Ch 4).

q.q: On which scalar does Ch 11 show a leak?
o: Volume–time: exhaled volume doesn't return to baseline
Flow–time: expiratory flow doesn't return to zero
Pressure–time: a spike appears at end-inspiration
Pressure–time: a dip appears before inspiration
q.e: Flow not returning to zero = auto-PEEP; volume not returning = leak.

q.q: What is the normal work of breathing range that both books share?
q.e: Hess 0.3–0.7, Heuer 0.5–0.7 J/L; 0.5–0.7 is the overlap.

q.q: Which loop should you 'think resistance' for?
q.e: "Volume/Pressure Loop = compliance; Flow/Volume Loop = resistance."

q.q: On a ventilator flow–volume loop, what does bronchospasm do to the expiratory limb?
o: Lowers peak expiratory flow and makes the limb flatter
Raises peak expiratory flow and makes the limb steeper
Leaves the limb unchanged; the inspiratory limb flattens
Makes the limb stop short of zero volume at end-exhalation
q.e: Inspiratory flow is preset; look at the expiratory limb.

q.q: How is bronchodilator response seen on a flow–volume loop?
o: Peak expiratory flow improves after the bronchodilator
Peak inspiratory flow falls after the bronchodilator
The loop no longer closes after the bronchodilator
Exhaled volume falls after the bronchodilator
q.e: Ch 11 Fig 11-10: compare before and after.

q.q: Which spirometry flow–volume shape fits obstruction?
o: A concave ('scooped') expiratory curve, L-shaped when severe
An 'upside-down ice cream cone' that is tall and narrow
A normal 'sail' shape with a straight expiratory limb
A tall, narrow curve with a normal peak flow and a small volume
q.e: Obstructive: concave downward; restrictive: tall narrow 'ice cream cone'.

q.q: Flow is reduced equally on inspiration and expiration. What does this suggest?
o: Fixed upper-airway obstruction such as tracheal stenosis
Variable extrathoracic obstruction such as vocal cord paralysis
Restrictive disease such as pulmonary fibrosis
Small-airway obstruction such as asthma or COPD
q.e: A variable lesion (vocal cord paralysis) reduces flow only on forced inhalation.

q.q: Which spirometry loop shape is restrictive?
o: An 'upside-down ice cream cone' with rapid emptying
A scooped 'ocean wave' with slow emptying and a long tail
A flattened top and bottom, like a box
A normal 'sail' with a low peak flow only
q.e: Hess Ch 8.

q.q: Which setting does RCP 105 say controls CO₂?
q.e: "Rate controls CO₂. FiO₂ and PEEP control oxygenation."

q.q: A ventilated patient has a respiratory acidosis. According to RCP 203, which of the following should be changed first?
o: Decrease the VT (keeping it above 4 mL/kg)
q.e: ↑ rate first; if that fails, ↑ VT within 4–8 mL/kg PBW and Pplat ≤ 30.

q.q: Will raising the FiO₂ lower a high PaCO₂?
q.e: Exam trap: raising FiO₂ does not lower PaCO₂.

q.q: A ventilated COPD patient has a PaCO₂ of 55 mm Hg and a pH of 7.37. Which of the following should be done?
o: Leave the PaCO₂ alone — the pH is normal
Increase the rate to bring the PaCO₂ to 40
Decrease the rate to raise the PaCO₂ further
Add 10 cm H₂O of PEEP to improve ventilation
q.e: In chronic CO₂ retention a normal pH can come with PaCO₂ ≥ 55; don't force it to 40.

q.q: Rate, VT and Pplat are at their limits and the pH is still below 7.30. What does RCP 203 allow?
o: An increase in the tidal volume to 12 mL/kg PBW
An increase in the Pplat limit to 45 cm H₂O
A change to CPAP with no pressure support
q.e: Let PaCO₂ rise as long as pH stays > 7.20–7.25.

q.q: Set rate 14, PaCO₂ 60, desired PaCO₂ 40. What is the new rate?
q.src: Calculating the new rate for a target PaCO₂

q.q: Why does raising the rate lower PaCO₂?
o: PaCO₂ varies inversely with alveolar ventilation
The rate increases the CO₂ produced by the muscles
The rate raises the FiO₂ delivered to the alveoli
The rate lowers the anatomic dead space to zero
q.e: With constant CO₂ production, ↑ V̇E lowers PaCO₂.
q.src: Calculating the new rate for a target PaCO₂

q.q: What is the risk of setting a very high rate in COPD?
o: Shortened expiratory time causing air trapping and auto-PEEP
Metabolic acidosis from increased renal bicarbonate loss
Hypoxemia from a lower delivered FiO₂
q.e: Too high a rate shortens TE → air trapping and auto-PEEP.
q.src: Calculating the new rate for a target PaCO₂

q.q: A ventilated patient has a low PaCO₂ compensating for diabetic ketoacidosis. What should be done?
o: Reduce the rate to normalize the PaCO₂
q.e: A compensatory PaCO₂ must not be normalized.
q.src: When the ABG says change the vent but you should not

q.q: A patient's PaCO₂ drops because they are hypoxic. What is the correct action?
o: Fix the hypoxia first; don't reduce ventilation
Reduce the rate first; then treat the hypoxia
Reduce the VT first; then check the SpO₂
Increase the pressure support and sedate
q.e: Low PaCO₂ as a response to hypoxia: fix the hypoxia.
q.src: When the ABG says change the vent but you should not

q.q: An ABG shows metabolic acidosis on the ventilator. What ventilator change is indicated?
o: None — don't increase support for a metabolic problem
Increase the rate until the pH returns to 7.40
Increase the FiO₂ and the PEEP
Decrease the VT and the flow
q.e: No ventilator adjustment for metabolic disorders; treat the cause.
q.src: When the ABG says change the vent but you should not

q.q: pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 50 from oversedation. What does the deck say?
o: Find and correct the cause; increasing the rate is not the proper action
Increase the rate at once; the cause of the acidosis can be found afterward
Decrease the FiO₂; oxygen is depressing the respiratory drive
Switch to CPAP; the patient needs to breathe spontaneously
q.e: For high PaCO₂ from oversedation or fatigue, correct the cause (e.g. delay weaning).
q.src: When the ABG says change the vent but you should not

q.q: Oxygenation is acceptable on less than 50% O₂. What should be adjusted to fine-tune it?
q.e: RCP 203: if acceptable on < 50% O₂, adjust FiO₂; if not, adjust PEEP.
q.src: Oxygenation targets, FiO₂ limits, FiO₂ vs PEEP

q.q: As oxygenation improves, which is lowered first?
q.e: Lower FiO₂ to ≤ 0.50 first, then PEEP.
q.src: Oxygenation targets, FiO₂ limits, FiO₂ vs PEEP

q.q: What FiO₂ ceiling should be used to avoid O₂ toxicity on this exam?
q.e: Conflict resolved: use < 50% (RCP 105 Initiation, and RCP 203's switch point).
q.src: Oxygenation targets, FiO₂ limits, FiO₂ vs PEEP

q.q: What PaO₂/SpO₂ goals apply in ARDS lung-protective ventilation?
q.e: ARDSNet goals: PaO₂ 55–80, SpO₂ 88–95%.
q.src: Oxygenation targets, FiO₂ limits, FiO₂ vs PEEP

q.q: A BiPAP patient on 10/5 needs better ventilation only. What is the NBRC change?
q.e: Ventilation only → ↑ IPAP, so ΔP rises and baseline stays.

q.q: A BiPAP patient on 10/5 needs better oxygenation and ventilation. What is the change?
q.e: Both → raise both, IPAP more than EPAP.

q.q: On BiPAP, which pressures adjust oxygenation?
q.e: Ventilation via IPAP/ΔP; oxygenation via FiO₂/EPAP.

q.q: PEEP 10 with FiO₂ 75% and PaO₂ 130. Which should be lowered first?
o: FiO₂ — oxygen toxicity is the concern
Neither — both are at safe levels
The rate — hyperventilation is the concern
q.e: Lower whichever is more dangerous: high FiO₂ → oxygen toxicity.

q.q: PEEP 18 with FiO₂ 45% and PaO₂ 120. Which should be lowered first?
o: FiO₂ — oxygen toxicity is the concern
The rate — air trapping is the concern
Neither — both are at safe levels
q.e: High PEEP with modest FiO₂ → PEEP is the concern.

q.q: PaO₂ 52 on FiO₂ 0.70. What does the 60-60 rule say?
q.e: PaO₂ < 60 on FiO₂ > 0.6 = shunt → PEEP/CPAP.

q.q: PaO₂ 55 on FiO₂ 0.35. What is the likely mechanism and fix?
q.e: FiO₂ below 0.6 → V/Q imbalance responds to a simple FiO₂ increase.

q.q: When VT is properly set (6–8 mL/kg PBW, Pplat < 30), what is preferred to change V̇E?
q.e: RR changes are the preferred method once VT is set correctly.

q.q: What ETT size does RCP 203 give for an adult man?
q.e: Deck: women 7.0–8.0, men 8.0–9.0 mm ID.

q.q: How are adult ETTs sized?
o: By sex, not height or weight
By height, not sex or weight
By weight, not sex or height
By age, not sex or weight
q.e: Adults are sized by sex; the LMA is sized by weight and the King LT by height.

q.q: What is the typical oral ETT depth at the teeth for a man?
q.e: Women 19–21, men 21–23 cm; confirm with CXR (tip 4–6 cm above carina).

q.q: Why is an ETT of 8 mm or larger preferred when possible?
o: An ETT raises WOB by 54–240% depending on size
A smaller ETT raises WOB by only 5–10%, whatever its size
A larger ETT lowers the risk of ventilator-associated pneumonia
A larger ETT seals the trachea without the need for a cuff
q.e: Bigger tubes reduce resistance and work of breathing.

q.q: What uncuffed ETT size does the formula give for a 4-year-old?
q.e: (age ÷ 4) + 4 = 1 + 4 = 5.0 mm; cuffed 4.5 mm.

q.q: What cuffed ETT size fits an 8-year-old?
What insertion depth from the lips does Hess give for children?
q.e: Depth = age + 10; a 4-year-old → 14 cm.

q.q: What is the Broselow Tape used for?
o: Length-based emergency equipment sizing for children ≤ 35 kg
Weight-based drug dosing for adults who weigh more than 35 kg
Measuring cuff pressure in pediatric endotracheal tubes
Measuring head circumference to estimate gestational age
q.e: A color-coded length-based tape recommends airways and equipment.

q.q: What ETT size does Hess give for a neonate weighing less than 1000 g?
q.src: Neonates: Size by Weight or Gestational Age

q.q: How deep is a neonatal ETT placed from the lips?
q.e: 1 kg → 7 cm; confirm by auscultation and chest x-ray.
q.src: Neonates: Size by Weight or Gestational Age

q.q: Which ETT is used for premature infants or infants under 3 kg?
q.e: RCP 203: uncuffed for premature or < 3 kg; cuffed now routine in older children.
q.src: Neonates: Size by Weight or Gestational Age

q.q: A neonate's weight is unknown but gestational age is 32 weeks. What ETT size fits?
q.src: Neonates: Size by Weight or Gestational Age

q.q: What is the purpose of diagnostic bronchoscopy?
o: To find out what's wrong — gather information or confirm a diagnosis
To fix the problem — remove a foreign body or a mucus plug
To open the airway — place a stent or dilate a stenosis
To stop bleeding — apply epinephrine, iced saline or a balloon tamponade
q.e: Diagnostic = Look; therapeutic = Treat.

q.q: Which is a THERAPEUTIC indication for bronchoscopy (RCP 203)?
o: Clearing mucus plugs causing lobar atelectasis
Evaluating a lung lesion of unknown etiology
Finding the source of unexplained hemoptysis
q.e: Therapeutic: difficult intubation, mucus plugs, foreign body/tissue removal, stents, balloon dilation.

q.q: Which is a DIAGNOSTIC indication for bronchoscopy?
o: Balloon dilatation of a tracheal stenosis
q.e: Diagnostic: unexplained cough/wheeze/stridor, CXR lesions, hemoptysis source, sampling.

q.q: Which three sedation drugs does the RCP 202 deck say to focus on?
q.e: Plus their reversal agents.

q.q: Which reversal agent can precipitate seizures and is not given routinely to speed recovery?
q.e: Flumazenil reverses midazolam but can precipitate seizures.

q.q: How is bleeding controlled through the bronchoscope?
o: Epinephrine, thrombin or iced saline via the working channel
Lidocaine 4%, acetylcysteine or albuterol via the working channel
Albuterol or ipratropium via an in-line nebulizer
Heparinized saline via the working channel
q.e: RCP 105 gives topical 1:1000 epinephrine; thrombin helps blood clot.

q.q: Why is lidocaine given before bronchoscopy?
o: It is a local anesthetic that suppresses cough
It is an anticholinergic that dries secretions
It is a bronchodilator that prevents wheezing
It is a vasoconstrictor that prevents bleeding
q.e: RCP 105: 5–10 mL of 1–4% via aerosol or through the channel.

q.q: What minimum NPO time before bronchoscopy does the Ch 16 deck give?
q.e: NPO ≥ 8 h before; ≥ 2 h after or until the gag reflex returns.

q.q: During bronchoscopy, a patient's SpO₂ falls below 90%. Which of the following should be done?
o: Increase the FiO₂ at once, or stop and give O₂ through the scope channel
Continue the procedure and recheck the SpO₂ when the scope is removed
Remove the supplemental oxygen and let the patient breathe room air
Give more sedation so that the patient tolerates the scope better
q.e: PaO₂ usually falls; always give O₂ and react to SpO₂ < 90%.

q.q: How is the scope passed in a ventilated patient?
o: Through the ETT via a Bodai or swivel-Y adaptor, so FiO₂ and PEEP continue
Through the ETT after disconnecting the ventilator, with apnea for the procedure
Through the nose beside the ETT, with the cuff deflated for the procedure
Through the mouth beside the ETT, with a bite block and the cuff inflated
q.e: The adaptor lets ventilation continue during the procedure.

q.q: Which special bronchoscopies reach peripheral lesions?
o: EBUS, electromagnetic navigation and robotic bronchoscopy
Rigid bronchoscopy confined to the trachea and main bronchi
q.e: EBUS, ENB and Ion robotic bronchoscopy can be combined.

q.q: Which labs rule out a bleeding disorder before a bronchoscopic biopsy?
o: INR, PT, PTT, CBC and platelet count
q.e: Ch 16: check INR, PT, PTT, CBC and platelets before biopsy.

q.q: What is the main purpose of a transtracheal oxygen catheter?
o: O₂ conservation by bypassing upper-airway dead space
Ventilation of apneic patients through the trachea
Suctioning of secretions below the vocal cords
Monitoring of PETCO₂ in spontaneously breathing patients
q.e: It delivers equivalent oxygenation at a lower continuous flow.

q.q: What is the key complication of a transtracheal O₂ catheter?
q.e: Humidification and catheter cleaning matter (RCP 202 Lssn 10).

q.q: How is a transtracheal catheter classed as an O₂ device?
q.e: Hess lists it with O₂-conserving devices; it also improves adherence because it's hidden.

q.q: Which patient may receive an oropharyngeal airway?
o: An unconscious patient without a gag reflex
A conscious patient with a strong gag reflex
A semi-conscious patient who is coughing
An awake patient with a basilar skull fracture
q.e: An OPA in a patient with a gag reflex causes gagging, vomiting and aspiration.

q.q: How is an OPA sized per RCP 203?
o: From the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw
From the tip of the nose to the earlobe
From the incisors to the thyroid notch
From the corner of the mouth to the tragus of the ear
q.e: Size by anatomy; too large presses the epiglottis, too small pushes the tongue back.

q.q: How is an OPA inserted in an infant?
o: Depress the tongue with a tongue depressor and insert directly, without rotation
Insert it upside down and rotate it 180° once the tip reaches the soft palate
Insert it sideways and rotate it 90° once it passes the base of the tongue
Lubricate it and pass it along the floor of the nose, without rotation
q.e: Adults: rotate 180°; infants/small children: no rotation.

q.q: Which patient is better suited to a nasopharyngeal airway than an OPA?
o: A semi-conscious patient with an intact gag reflex
An apneic patient with no gag reflex
A patient with significant midface trauma and epistaxis
A patient with a basilar skull fracture
q.e: NPAs are better tolerated with a gag reflex.

q.q: How is an NPA sized per RCP 203?
o: From the nares to the earlobe (or tragus)
From the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw
From the nares to the thyroid cartilage
From the bridge of the nose to the chin
q.e: Choose the largest diameter that passes without force.

q.q: What is the major contraindication to an NPA?
o: Suspected basilar skull fracture or significant midface trauma
An intact gag reflex in a semi-conscious patient who needs suctioning
A need for frequent nasotracheal suctioning
A conscious patient with trismus (clenched jaw)
q.e: Complications: laryngospasm, nosebleeds, sinus infection with prolonged use.

q.q: Where does an LMA sit?
o: Above the glottis, sealing around the laryngeal inlet
In the trachea, sealing below the vocal cords
In the esophagus, sealing below the larynx
In the nasopharynx, sealing behind the soft palate and uvula
q.e: Supraglottic; it does not enter the trachea.

q.q: What LMA size fits a 60-kg adult per the deck?
q.e: Size 4 = 50–70 kg; size 5 = 70–100 kg.

q.q: What is the maximum LMA cuff pressure?
q.e: LMA cuff ≤ 60 (an ETT cuff is 20–30).

q.q: What is the main limitation of an LMA compared with a cuffed ETT?
o: It cannot be used during anesthesia
It requires a view of the vocal cords
q.e: The LMA protects less against aspiration.

q.q: A patient with an LMA in place regurgitates. Which of the following should be done?
o: Leave it in, position head-down or side-lying, suction, prepare to intubate
Remove the LMA at once, sit the patient upright and suction the mouth
Inflate the cuff with more air, then continue to ventilate as before
Increase the ventilating pressure to keep the fluid out of the trachea
q.e: RCP 203: don't remove it; position, disconnect, suction, prepare to intubate.

q.q: What is probably the most common reason for a tracheostomy?
q.e: Three reasons: bypass upper obstruction, remove secretions, long-term ventilation.

q.q: What must be done before capping a fenestrated trach or placing a speaking valve?
o: Remove the inner cannula and keep the cuff up
q.e: Never cap or place a speaking valve with the cuff inflated.

q.q: What should be kept at the bedside after tracheostomy insertion?
o: The obturator and a spare inner cannula
A cuffed tube two sizes larger
A suction catheter and saline alone
An LMA and a bite block
q.e: Remove the obturator immediately after insertion and keep it at the bedside.

q.q: What is a tracheostomy button?
o: A short cannula that keeps the stoma open without a full tube
A cuffed tracheostomy tube used for long-term ventilation
A one-way speaking valve that fits on the tube
A suction port above the cuff of a trach tube
q.e: It has no cuff, so PPV leaks; it is not a secure airway.

q.q: A Combitube is placed blindly. Which lumen should be ventilated first?
q.e: "BLUE FIRST": it usually lands in the esophagus; switch to clear if in the trachea.

q.q: Where does the King LT tip normally sit?
q.e: The distal cuff blocks the esophagus; gas exits between the cuffs toward the larynx.

q.q: What is the definitive tracheal airway in the deck's ladder?
q.e: OPA/NPA basic; King/Combitube/LMA supraglottic rescue; ETT definitive.

q.q: A ventilated patient's ETT becomes obstructed. Which of the following is the first step?
o: Remove the patient from the ventilator and manually ventilate with 100% O₂
Increase the ventilator pressure limit and continue mechanical ventilation
Wait and observe to see whether the obstruction clears with a cough
Remove the tube at once and place a nasal cannula at 6 L/min
q.e: Then reassess; try an airway exchange catheter through the blocked tube if available.

q.q: A fresh tracheostomy tube comes out of the stoma. Which of the following should be done?
o: Call for help, cover the stoma with petroleum gauze, BVM-ventilate with O₂
Reinsert the same tube at once through the fresh stoma, without calling for help
Leave the stoma open to air and observe the patient's SpO₂
Insert a nasopharyngeal airway into the stoma and ventilate
q.e: A fresh stoma can close or misdirect a tube.

q.q: After a failed intubation attempt, SpO₂ falls below 90% and BVM fails. What next?
o: Make up to 5 more intubation attempts
Stop ventilating and wait for help
Give more sedation and a paralytic
q.e: CICO: supraglottic airway; if that fails, emergency surgical airway.

q.q: What is the only absolute contraindication to intubation?
q.e: Ch 16: relative contraindications include airway trauma, C-spine injury, Mallampati 4.

q.q: What does Mallampati class IV show?
o: Only the hard palate — most difficult
Soft palate, uvula and pillars — easiest
Soft palate and base of uvula — difficult
q.e: Class I easiest → class IV most difficult.

q.q: How long should each intubation attempt last?
q.e: Call out the time; resume bagging with 100% O₂ between attempts.

q.q: A colorimetric CO₂ detector turns yellow with each exhalation. What does this mean?
o: CO₂ is detected — consistent with tracheal placement
No CO₂ is detected — the tube is in the esophagus
The detector is wet and must be replaced
The patient is hypoxemic and needs a higher FiO₂
q.e: Purple (< 0.5%) → yellow (≥ 2%); in cardiac arrest it may stay purple despite correct placement.

q.q: Can CO₂ detection identify a mainstem intubation?
o: No — record the depth and confirm with a chest x-ray
Yes — a mainstem tube gives no color change
Yes — but with waveform capnography alone
No — auscultate over the stomach to confirm the depth instead
q.e: CO₂ confirms tracheal, not mainstem, placement.

q.q: Which position is used for intubation without suspected C-spine injury?
q.e: Neck slightly flexed, head extended; with suspected C-spine injury use MILS.

q.q: How long is each postural drainage position held?
q.e: Deck and Hess: 5–10 min per position; sessions 20–40 min.
q.src: Manual Percussion, Vibration and Postural Drainage

q.q: In postural drainage, how is the affected segment positioned?
o: Up, so gravity moves mucus to the larger airways
Down, so the weight of the lung squeezes the mucus out
Level with the heart, so blood flow matches ventilation
Toward the feet, so the mucus moves away from the trachea
q.e: Gravity drains the elevated segment toward the larger airways.
q.src: Manual Percussion, Vibration and Postural Drainage

q.q: When should postural drainage be stopped?
o: When sputum drops below 30 mL/day with an effective cough
When sputum exceeds 30 mL/day with an effective cough
After the first session, whatever the sputum volume
When the chest radiograph has been clear for 30 days
q.e: Sputum > 30 mL/day indicates airway clearance; stop when below with effective cough.
q.src: Manual Percussion, Vibration and Postural Drainage

q.q: When should CPT sessions be timed?
q.e: Deck: before meals or 2 h after (Hess says > 1 h).
q.src: Manual Percussion, Vibration and Postural Drainage

q.q: Which is a contraindication to postural drainage and percussion?
q.e: Also recent spinal surgery, uncontrolled hypertension; no head-down with gross hemoptysis.
q.src: Manual Percussion, Vibration and Postural Drainage

q.q: How does the deck compare mechanical percussors with cupped hands?
o: Equally effective, with consistent force and no user fatigue
Less effective, with inconsistent force and more user fatigue
More effective, with greater force and more rib fractures
Equally effective, but not safe for use in children
q.e: Deck: equally effective; Hess says data are lacking.

q.q: What is HFCWO (the vest)?
o: An inflatable vest giving rapid positive-pressure bursts at about 5–20 Hz
A mask that gives positive expiratory pressure of about 5–20 cm H₂O on each breath
A mouthpiece device that oscillates the airflow at about 5–20 Hz
A manual technique of clapping the chest at about 5–20 Hz
q.e: Used mainly for CF and bronchiectasis, especially at home without caregiver help.

q.q: Which therapy does the deck say replaced IPPB?
q.e: IPV gives high-flow mini-bursts with aerosol at 300–400 pulses/min.

q.q: What does the Metaneb combine?
o: Continuous PEP for lung expansion and high-frequency oscillation for secretions
Heliox for better airflow and inhaled nitric oxide for pulmonary vasodilation
Suction for secretions and saline lavage for mucus plugs
Oxygen for hypoxemia and heated humidity for secretions
q.e: CPEP + CHFO with aerosol; can run in-line with a ventilator.

q.q: What pressure range do PEP devices typically create during exhalation?
q.e: PEP: 6–25 cm H₂O on exhalation with unrestricted inspiration.

q.q: To mobilize secretions, which PEP device is probably the best choice?
q.e: Vibratory PEP (Flutter, Acapella) helps mobilize secretions.

q.q: How does the Acapella differ from the Flutter?
o: The Acapella works independently of gravity
The Acapella must be held at a specific angle
The Acapella uses a steel ball in a cone
q.e: Flutter: steel ball, gravity-dependent; Acapella: lever and magnet, any position.

q.q: Which is a contraindication to PEP therapy?
q.e: Also high ICP, hemodynamic instability, bullous emphysema, sinusitis, middle-ear problems.

q.q: How many sets are done in a PEP session per the deck?
o: Sets of 10–20 breaths repeated 4–8 times, ≤ 20 minutes
One set of 5 breaths, repeated every hour while awake
Sets of 50–100 breaths repeated 2 times, ≤ 60 minutes
Continuous breathing through the device for an hour
q.e: Directed cough after each set.

q.q: What is IPPB's status on NBRC exams per the deck?
o: Removed — no longer recommended and replaced by IPV
The first-line lung-expansion therapy after surgery
Required for all postoperative patients who cannot cough
Recommended for aerosol delivery in acute asthma
q.e: Use the deck: IPPB is off the exam and replaced by IPV.

q.q: How is an IPPB machine classified (Hess)?
q.e: Patient-triggered, passively inflating the lungs.

q.q: Should IPPB be used for aerosol therapy (Hess)?
q.e: Hess: IPPB should not be used for aerosol therapy.

q.q: What does IPV deliver?
o: Rapid short bursts of pressurized air combined with aerosol
Continuous high PEEP with a fixed inspiratory pressure
A single large breath held for 5–10 seconds
Slow deep breaths of heliox combined with aerosol
q.e: IPV mobilizes mucus, opens airways and improves lung expansion.
q.src: What IPV Is and How It Works

q.q: What rate should be used on the exam for IPV?
q.e: Deck and glossary: > 200 cycles/min (Hess text 300–400).
q.src: What IPV Is and How It Works

q.q: What is IPV's key advantage over IPPB?
o: It combines airway clearance and lung expansion in one therapy
It costs less to deliver and needs no compressed gas source
It gives a larger tidal volume with each breath
It can be used by children without supervision
q.e: The deck says IPPB has been replaced by IPV.
q.src: What IPV Is and How It Works

q.q: How is exhalation achieved during IPV (Hess)?
o: By the oscillator pulling gas out
q.e: The patient keeps breathing spontaneously during the oscillations.
q.src: What IPV Is and How It Works

q.q: How long is a typical MetaNeb session?
q.e: MetaNeb: CPEP (expansion) and CHFO (clearance) with aerosol.

q.q: Which percussive device cannot be used with a ventilator?
q.e: PercussiveNeb: 11–30 Hz, single-patient use, not with a ventilator.

q.q: What are the two MetaNeb modes per RCP 203?
o: CPEP for lung expansion and CHFO for secretion clearance
PEEP for oxygenation and PS for ventilation
IPAP for ventilation and EPAP for oxygenation
CPAP for lung expansion and IPV for aerosol delivery
q.e: It can run in-line with a ventilator.

q.q: Which is a contraindication to IPV?
q.e: Also active hemoptysis, recent facial/oral surgery, unstable CV status, elevated ICP.

q.q: What does the CF Foundation recommend about airway clearance?
o: Regular ACT for all CF patients, individualized — no therapy shown superior
IPV for all CF patients, since it has been shown to be superior
No airway clearance unless there is an acute exacerbation
Head-down postural drainage for all CF patients, twice daily for life
q.e: Individualize by age, preference and adverse events.

q.q: Which risk does RCP 203 cite for no longer placing CF patients head-down for postural drainage?
q.e: RCP 203 Lssn 6b.

q.q: How much of the ETT internal diameter may an adult suction catheter occlude?
q.e: < 50% for adults, < 70% for infants, so gas can flow around it.
q.src: How to Pick the Catheter Size

q.q: What suction catheter fits a 6.0-mm ETT per the deck?
q.e: 2 × 6 = 12, then the next smallest size = 10 Fr.
q.src: How to Pick the Catheter Size

q.q: What suction catheter fits an 8.0-mm ETT using the deck's rule?
q.e: 2 × 8 = 16 → next smallest = 14 Fr.
q.src: How to Pick the Catheter Size

q.q: What does a French size measure?
o: The outer circumference (Fr ≈ diameter in mm × 3)
The inner diameter in mm (Fr ≈ diameter × 2)
The length of the catheter in cm (Fr ≈ length ÷ 3)
The maximum suction pressure (Fr ≈ mm Hg ÷ 10)
q.e: Hess: Fr ≈ diameter (mm) × 3.
q.src: How to Pick the Catheter Size

q.q: What suction pressure range does the deck give for adults?
q.e: Children −80 to −100; infants −60 to −80.

q.q: What suction pressure range is used for infants?
q.e: Use the deck's Ch 10 ranges.

q.q: How long may each suction attempt last?
q.e: Use 15 s (RCP 105 says 10 s).

q.q: How should a patient be oxygenated before suctioning (Ch 11)?
q.e: Hess: FiO₂ 1.0; neonates +0.1 for 30–60 s.

q.q: What continuous suction pressure does a CASS (subglottic) port use?
q.e: Continuous low suction removes pooled secretions above the cuff.
